title: I Built an AI Tutor That Isn't Allowed to Help
author: Greg O'Keefe
summary: Greg O'Keefe identifies a structural flaw in both tutoring and classroom teaching: the tutor explains, the student nods, both feel progress, but the understanding belongs to the tutor, not the student. He calls this the Reconstruction Problem -- the 40-50% of tutoring sessions consumed re-establishing plot, vocabulary, and comprehension gaps the student should have arrived with, crowding out the interpretive and argumentative work that actually prepares students for exams. To address this, O'Keefe built Project Zeno, an AI tutoring system governed by the Non-Substitution Rule: Zeno is forbidden from doing cognitive work the student should do. Instead of explaining, Zeno asks. The system uses a four-step protocol -- Identify, Attempt, Support, Confirm -- that forces student reconstruction rather than passive reception. A key design element is the Ascent Consolidation Protocol, which requires students to articulate what they now understand before the session can advance. This prevents the illusion of progress that surfaces when a student nods at an explanation but cannot reproduce the reasoning. The system is deliberately Socratic: its value comes entirely from what it refuses to do. O'Keefe reports that initial results show reduced reconstruction time and improved student ownership of comprehension work, and argues the Non-Substitution Rule points toward a broader principle -- the most powerful educational technology may be one that enforces productive difficulty rather than providing convenient answers.
points: The tutoring session's core failure mode is that explanation feels like progress to both parties -- the tutor feels helpful, the student feels understood -- but received understanding does not transfer to independent performance under exam conditions.

The Non-Substitution Rule is Zeno's architectural heart: the system must never perform cognitive work (summarising, interpreting, explaining) that the student is capable of doing with support -- every explanation substituted is a transfer opportunity destroyed.

The Identify-Attempt-Support-Confirm protocol operationalises productive struggle: students name the gap, attempt the answer, receive scaffolding only after failing, then confirm comprehension in their own words before advancing.

The Ascent Consolidation Protocol blocks the most dangerous tutoring illusion -- the session-end nod -- by requiring students to articulate understanding before the system counts a concept as mastered.

O'Keefe's design implies a principle applicable beyond AI: the most valuable educational tools are not those that make learning easier but those that preserve the friction necessary for genuine transfer.
quotes: The student stalls. The tutor explains. The student nods. The tutor feels the session moving forward. The student feels like they understand. They don't. They received the understanding. That's different.

Between 40 and 50% of a typical secondary tutoring session is consumed by what I started calling reconstruction work: re-establishing plot, rebuilding vocabulary, filling comprehension gaps the student should have arrived with after reading. That's not instruction. That's scaffolding for scaffolding.

Zeno is not allowed to explain. It is not allowed to summarize. It is not allowed to tell the student what the text means, what the author intended, or what the correct interpretation is. Every one of those moves, if Zeno makes it, substitutes Zeno's cognition for the student's.

The Non-Substitution Rule works because explanation is the path of least resistance. The tutor can always explain. The explanation will always make sense to the tutor. The student will almost always nod. This is the trap.

The Ascent Consolidation Protocol requires students to articulate what they now understand before the session advances. Not a nod. Not a 'yes'. A sentence, in their words, demonstrating that the comprehension happened inside them and not inside the room.

What I've found is that the hardest part of building Zeno wasn't the technology. It was enforcing the rule on myself. Every time a student is stuck, there is a strong pull to just explain. Zeno doesn't feel that pull. That's why it works.
